lesson.title: Four Tax Numbers and Two Kinds of Differences
lesson.summary: A company works out profit twice: once under accounting rules for its financial statements and once under tax rules for the tax return. This lesson shows how the four tax-related numbers differ and why only some gaps between the two profits ever reverse.

sections.heading: Two rulebooks, two profits
sections.body_markdown: Think of a student graded by the school and also scored by a sports league. Both look at the same performance, but each has its own rules, so the scores differ. A company is in the same position. **Accounting profit** (also called pretax income or profit before tax) is measured with financial reporting standards and appears on the income statement. **Taxable income** is measured with the tax authority's rules and appears on the tax return. The two usually differ because tax law recognizes some revenues and expenses at different times, or not at all.

sections.heading: Taxes payable versus income tax expense
sections.body_markdown: **Taxes payable** (current tax) is what the company owes the tax authority for the year: $\text{taxable income} \times \text{tax rate}$. It is a balance sheet amount. **Income tax expense** is the tax cost shown on the income statement. It is built from taxes payable plus a *deferred tax* adjustment for timing differences that will reverse later. Taxes payable follows the tax return, while income tax expense follows the accounting profit. The two match only when no timing differences exist. Do not confuse either with cash taxes actually paid, which also depends on payment dates and installments.

sections.heading: Permanent differences: never reversing
sections.body_markdown: A **permanent difference** is an item that enters accounting profit or taxable income but never enters the other. Typical examples are a dividend that is accounting income but not taxable, and a fine or a club membership that is an accounting expense but not tax-deductible. Tax-exempt income is *subtracted* when moving from accounting profit to taxable income, and non-deductible expenses are *added back*. These items change taxes payable and the tax expense together. They create no deferred tax, because nothing comes back later.

sections.heading: Temporary differences: timing only
sections.body_markdown: A **temporary difference** is an item recognized in a different period for accounting than for tax. It reverses in a later period, so over the item's life the two totals agree. Examples are faster tax depreciation than book depreciation, a warranty cost accrued now but deductible only when paid, and rent collected in advance that is taxed on receipt but earned later. A temporary difference moves taxes payable away from the tax rate times accounting profit, and the deferred tax part of income tax expense then makes up the gap. The key test is whether the item will reverse. Size and recurrence do not matter.

worked_example.problem: A company reports pretax income (accounting profit) of $500,000 and the tax rate is 30%. The figure includes $20,000 of dividend income that is never taxable. It also includes a $10,000 fine that is never deductible. Book depreciation is $80,000 while tax depreciation is $140,000. A $30,000 warranty expense was accrued and none has been paid, and tax law allows the deduction only when it is paid. Assume there are no opening deferred tax balances. Find taxable income, taxes payable, and income tax expense.
steps: Permanent differences: subtract the non-taxable dividend ($20,000) and add back the non-deductible fine ($10,000). That is a net change of −$10,000, giving $490,000.
Temporary difference 1: tax depreciation exceeds book depreciation by $140,000 − $80,000 = $60,000, so taxable income is lower. Subtract $60,000 to get $430,000.
Temporary difference 2: the warranty cost is expensed for accounting but not yet deductible, so add back $30,000 to get $460,000. This is taxable income.
Taxes payable = $460,000 × 30% = $138,000. On the calculator, enter 460000 × .3 =.
The two temporary differences net to a $30,000 reduction in taxable income now, which will reverse later. The deferred tax expense is $30,000 × 30% = $9,000.
Check: only the permanent differences cause expense to differ from pretax income × rate. ($500,000 − $20,000 + $10,000) × 30% = $147,000, which matches.
worked_example.answer: Taxable income is $460,000, taxes payable is $138,000, and income tax expense is $147,000 (of which $9,000 is deferred).

formulas.name: Taxable income
formulas.where: TI is taxable income, PBT is accounting profit before tax. Subtract tax-exempt income and add back non-deductible expenses. Adjust for timing items so that TI follows tax rules.

formulas.name: Taxes payable (current tax)
formulas.where: TI is taxable income and t is the tax rate that applies to the year.

formulas.name: Income tax expense
formulas.where: Deferred tax expense is the tax effect of temporary differences that arose or reversed this period. It is negative (a benefit) when earlier temporary differences reverse in the opposite direction.

exam_traps: Computing taxes payable as accounting profit × tax rate instead of taxable income × tax rate.
Adding tax-exempt income or subtracting non-deductible expenses. The direction is the opposite: exempt income comes out of taxable income and non-deductible costs are added back.
Treating income tax expense as the cash tax paid or as equal to taxes payable. The two match only when there are no temporary differences.
Classifying an item as temporary because it is large or happens every year. The test is whether it reverses; an item that never reverses is permanent.
Assuming permanent differences are ignored in the tax expense. They change both taxes payable and income tax expense, and they create no deferred tax.
builds_on: Accrual accounting and timing of recognition
leads_to: Effective, statutory and cash tax rates

mcqs.stem: Which description of taxes payable (current tax) for a period is most accurate?

options.text: Accounting profit before tax multiplied by the applicable tax rate
options.explanation: This uses accounting profit instead of taxable income, so it ignores both permanent and temporary differences.

options.text: Taxable income from the tax return multiplied by the applicable tax rate
options.explanation: Correct. Taxes payable is the amount owed on the tax return, which is taxable income times the rate.

options.text: The income tax expense shown on the income statement for the period
options.explanation: This confuses taxes payable with income tax expense. The expense also includes a deferred tax component.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is a permanent difference between accounting profit and taxable income?

options.text: A regulatory fine that is expensed but never allowed as a tax deduction
options.explanation: Correct. The item is in accounting profit and is never deductible, so it never reverses.

options.text: A warranty provision accrued now but deductible for tax only when paid
options.explanation: This is a timing difference. The deduction arrives later, so it is a temporary difference.

options.text: Tax depreciation that is faster than book depreciation on an asset
options.explanation: Total depreciation is the same over the life and only the timing differs, so it is temporary.

mcqs.stem: A company has pretax income of $400,000, which includes $50,000 of dividend income that is permanently exempt from tax. There are no other differences and the tax rate is 25%. Taxes payable for the year is closest to:

options.explanation: This is $400,000 × 25%. It ignores the permanent difference and applies the rate to accounting profit.
This adds the exempt dividend instead of subtracting it: $450,000 × 25%. It is a direction error.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about temporary differences is correct?

options.text: They never change the taxable income of the period in which they arise
options.explanation: They do change taxable income in the period they arise. Timing items are adjusted when moving from accounting profit to taxable income.

options.text: They reverse in later periods, so the item's total effect is the same under both rule sets
options.explanation: Correct. The timing differs, but the cumulative amount recognized for tax and for accounting converges once the item reverses.

options.text: They arise when an item is in accounting profit but is never taxed
options.explanation: This describes a permanent difference, not a temporary one. Temporary differences reverse.

mcqs.stem: A company has pretax income of $600,000 and a tax rate of 30%. The only difference between accounting and tax rules is a $20,000 fine that is expensed but never deductible. There are no temporary differences. Income tax expense is closest to:

options.explanation: Correct. Taxable income is $620,000 and taxes payable is $186,000. With no temporary differences there is no deferred tax, so the expense equals $186,000.
This is $600,000 × 30%. It ignores the permanent difference, which affects both taxes payable and the expense.
This subtracts the fine ($580,000 × 30%). The non-deductible expense must be added back.

mcqs.stem: A company has pretax income of $400,000 and a tax rate of 25%. It accrued a $40,000 warranty expense that tax law allows as a deduction only when paid, and none has been paid. There are no other differences and no opening deferred tax balances. Income tax expense is closest to:

options.explanation: This is the taxes payable on taxable income of $440,000. It leaves out the deferred tax benefit, so it mistakes taxes payable for the expense.
This subtracts the accrual from pretax income ($360,000 × 25%). The accrual is added back for taxable income, and the expense still follows accounting profit.
Correct. Taxes payable is $440,000 × 25% = $110,000. The temporary difference gives a $10,000 deferred tax benefit, so the expense is $100,000. This equals pretax income × rate.

mcqs.stem: Over the full life of the item, which situation leaves cumulative taxable income different from cumulative accounting profit?

options.text: Tax depreciation that is faster than book depreciation on an asset
options.explanation: Faster early deductions are offset by smaller deductions later, so the cumulative totals match. It is a temporary difference.

options.text: Dividend income that is recognized in profit each year but is exempt from tax
options.explanation: Correct. The income is never taxed, so it never reverses and the cumulative totals stay different. It is a permanent difference.

options.text: Rent received in advance that is taxed when received but earned next year
options.explanation: Tax recognizes the revenue first and accounting recognizes it later. Both eventually include it, so it is a temporary difference.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between accounting profit and taxable income?
flashcards.back: Accounting profit (pretax income) follows financial reporting standards and is shown on the income statement. Taxable income follows tax law and is shown on the tax return. They differ because of permanent and temporary differences.

flashcards.front: How are taxes payable and income tax expense each determined?
flashcards.back: Taxes payable = taxable income × tax rate, the amount owed for the year. Income tax expense = taxes payable + deferred tax expense, the cost shown on the income statement.

flashcards.front: Permanent versus temporary difference: what is the key contrast?
flashcards.back: A permanent difference is an item in one profit measure but never in the other, so it never reverses and creates no deferred tax. A temporary difference is a timing difference that reverses in a later period.

flashcards.front: Which way do you adjust accounting profit for tax-exempt income and for non-deductible expenses?
flashcards.back: Subtract tax-exempt income and add back non-deductible expenses when moving from accounting profit to taxable income.
